newsitem.title: USA: SEC charges ex-Tyson chairman with insider trading.
newsitem.headline: SEC charges ex-Tyson chairman with insider trading.

text.p: The Securities and Exchange Commission said Monday it filed insider trading charges against the former chairman of Tyson Foods Inc. and a friend in connection with the poultry company's purchase of Arctic Alaska Fisheries Corp. in 1992.

In a civil complaint filed in federal district court in Arkansas, the SEC alleged that Frederick Lee Cameron, bought Arctic Alaska shares based on a tip he received from his friend, Donald John Tyson, then chairman and majority shareholder of Tyson Foods.
Springdale, Ark.-based Tyson Foods is the nation's biggest poultry processor with sales of $5.5 billion last year.
Arctic Alaska is a Seattle-based seafoods processor that was traded at the New York Stock Exchange before being acquired by Tyson Foods in the $212 million deal.
Simultaneously with the filing of the complaint, Tyson and Cameron agreed to settle the charges, without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, the agency said.
Pending final court approval, the defendants consented to be permanently enjoined from violating anti-fraud provisions of federal securiies laws, the SEC said.
Cameron also agreed to forfeit $46,125, the alleged illegal profits, and pay interest totalling $18,153. Both Cameron and Tyson also agreed to each pay a civil penalty of $46,125, the SEC said.

Tyson, 66, lived in Fayetteville, Ark., at the time. He now resides in Miami, the SEC said. In late May and early June 1992, he took a trip with Cameron, 62, and a National City, Calif., resident, to Britain.
During the trip the food company official allegedly communicated with his office about the on-going negotiations with Arctic Alaska and participated at a board meeting on May 29 by phone.
According to the SEC lawsuit, Cameron bought 9,000 shares of Arctic Alaska at $6.625 a share or $59,625 on June 2, 1992, after receiving information from Tyson about the pending acquisition.
In doing so, Tyson violated his company's insider trading policy and breached his fiduciary duty to Arctic Alaska shareholders, the SEC contended.
Cameron sold the shares on June 16, the day the deal was announced, at $11.75 a share or $105,750, making a profit of $46,125, the SEC alleged.
